key_terms.meaning: A geographic area in which a provider runs one or more data centres; you pick a region to be near your users.
The round-trip time for a request to reach a server and come back; measured in milliseconds (ms) and set mostly by physical distance and the number of hops.
A company that carries your traffic to the wider Internet; the path usually passes through a local ISP, a regional ISP and a backbone provider.
A shared facility where ISPs and cloud providers connect directly, so traffic between them skips long backbone routes and latency drops.
The request-response text protocol of the web; a client sends a method (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) and a URL, the server returns a status code and a body.
The naming system that maps a name such as api.example.com to an IP address, using cached records with a TTL in seconds.
One running copy of software and one database schema (or one set of tables) serves many customers, with each tenant's data kept logically separate by a tenant ID.
A design style where business functions are packaged as separate, loosely coupled services that talk through a published, standard contract.
The published description of what a service accepts and returns (its operations, message formats and endpoint), so callers need no knowledge of the internals.
An HTTP style where every thing is a resource with a URL, standard methods act on it, and each request carries all the state needed (it is stateless).
Automatic addition or removal of capacity in response to measured demand, held between a minimum and a maximum size.
A rule of the form: if metric M stays above threshold T for W seconds, add N instances, subject to min and max limits and a cooldown period.
A device or service that receives client requests and forwards each one to a healthy backend, using a policy such as round robin or least connections.
Keeping extra, identical copies of a service or data set, on the same site or a different site, so a lost copy does not stop the service.
The switch of traffic from a failed copy to a healthy copy, done manually or automatically by a health check plus a load balancer or DNS change.
The contract between provider and customer that states the promised service level, how it is measured, and the credit or penalty if it is missed.
An internal, stricter target (for example 99.95% when the SLA promises 99.9%) that leaves headroom before a contract breach.
The fraction of time a service is usable, often written in nines: 99.9% allows about 43 minutes of downtime in a 30-day month.
A software-defined computer with its own virtual CPU, memory and disk, created and destroyed in seconds by a hypervisor on a physical host.
The metering function that records resource consumption (vCPU-hours, GB-months, requests) per tenant, which the billing system turns into a bill.

takeaways: A cloud region is a physical building with power, cooling, racks and switches, so distance and network hops set the floor on latency.
Users reach cloud software through DNS to find the address and HTTP to carry the request, which is why web standards decide much of cloud behaviour.
Multitenancy is what makes cloud cheap: one running stack serves many customers, and correctness depends on separating their data by tenant ID.
SOA turns business functions into loosely coupled services with contracts; REST is the lighter HTTP-based style most public cloud APIs now use.
Elasticity means capacity follows measured demand automatically, but always inside a minimum and maximum the operator has chosen.
A load balancer, health checks, replication and failover work as one team: spread traffic, detect a dead copy, and move traffic away from it.
An SLA is the promise a customer can claim against; an SLO is the tighter internal target that keeps you safely inside the SLA.
Virtual servers, virtual storage and usage monitors are the metered units, so every elastic action you take also changes the bill.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to define the mechanism, draw the request path or architecture, and then argue trade-offs (cost, latency, availability, lock-in) with a concrete example.

bank.q: Define multitenancy. Explain, with a diagram, how one running SaaS stack can serve many customers while keeping their data separate.
outline: Definition: one instance of software serves many tenants
Logical separation using tenant ID on every row or a schema per tenant
Authentication maps each request to exactly one tenant
Noisy-neighbour problem: one tenant's load affects others, so quotas are needed
Advantages: lower cost per user, single upgrade path; risk: one bug can expose many tenants

bank.q: Describe the chain a request travels from a user's phone to a cloud data centre, and explain how that chain affects latency and availability.
outline: Phone to Wi-Fi or mobile network to local ISP
ISP to regional ISP or backbone; exchange point (IXP) where networks meet
Provider edge router, then load balancer, then server inside the region
Each hop adds delay; distance sets a minimum latency
Any single hop or ISP failure breaks the path, so multi-region and CDN help

bank.q: Explain the roles of a load balancer, resource replication and a failover system in a highly available cloud service.
outline: Load balancer spreads requests and removes unhealthy backends
Health check: periodic probe, N failures mark a backend out
Replication keeps an identical copy of service or data
Failover switches traffic or promotes a standby copy
Together they remove single points of failure; state must be shared or replicated

bank.q: Distinguish between an SLA and an SLO. Give an example of each for a payment API and explain why the SLO is kept stricter.
outline: SLA: contract, customer-facing, credit or penalty
SLO: internal target, engineering-facing
Example: SLA 99.9% with service credits, SLO 99.95%
Headroom absorbs measurement noise, maintenance and short incidents
Error budget: the gap between SLO and SLA is the allowed failure

bank.q: List the resources a cloud usage monitor typically meters for a virtual server and for block storage, and state the usual billing units.
outline: Compute: vCPU-hours or instance-hours, GB-hours of memory
Storage: GB-months of provisioned or used disk
Network: GB out, number of requests
Snapshots and public IP addresses billed separately
Meter records feed the billing system per tenant per period

bank.q: An auto-scaling policy is: if average CPU stays above 65% for 3 minutes, add 2 instances, up to a maximum of 10, with a 5-minute cooldown. Starting from 4 instances, trace the steps for a traffic surge and for the later fall in traffic.
outline: Metric window: 3 minutes above 65% triggers one scale-out action
Add 2 instances: 4 to 6; cooldown blocks further actions for 5 minutes
Repeat until 10; the maximum limit caps cost
Scale-in uses a lower threshold so it does not flap
Warm-up time means new instances do not help instantly; state the risk of scaling on a lagging metric

bank.q: Design a small REST API for a railway ticket-booking service. Name the resources, the methods and status codes, and explain why the design is stateless.
outline: Resources: /trains, /trains/{id}, /bookings, /bookings/{id}
GET to read, POST to create a booking, DELETE to cancel
Status codes: 200, 201, 404, 409 for seat conflict, 400 for bad input
No client session on the server; a token carries identity on every call
Idempotency for retries; versioning of the API

bank.q: A service promises 99.9% availability in its SLA and runs to an internal SLO of 99.95%. Calculate the allowed downtime per 30-day month for both, and state the size of the internal error budget.
outline: 30 days = 720 hours = 43200 minutes
99.9% allows 0.1% of 43200 = 43.2 minutes
99.95% allows 0.05% = 21.6 minutes
Error budget for the team = 21.6 minutes; gap to the contract = 21.6 minutes
Discuss that planned maintenance is usually excluded from the SLA count

bank.q: Four identical web servers sit behind a load balancer. Describe, step by step, what happens when server 3 stops responding, and what the user sees at each stage.
outline: Health check fails after the configured number of attempts
Load balancer removes server 3 from the pool; no new requests go to it
In-flight requests on server 3 fail or time out; retry to a healthy node
Remaining three servers carry the load; capacity check against peak
Server 3 replaced by auto-scaling; it rejoins after passing health checks

bank.q: A SaaS product serves 200 small firms. Compare a shared table with a tenant ID column against one schema per tenant for isolation, cost and upgrade effort.
outline: Shared table: cheapest, one schema to migrate, needs every query filtered by tenant ID
One schema per tenant: stronger isolation, easier export and delete, many schemas to migrate
Per-tenant database is costlier but suits regulated customers
Noisy neighbour still possible on shared hardware; quotas and rate limits
Migration and reporting complexity named for each option

bank.q: A team wants to move an existing SOAP/WSDL service estate to REST APIs. Evaluate the change: what is gained, what is lost, and what should not be migrated.
outline: SOA strengths: formal contract, transactions, WS-Security, tooling for typed clients
REST gains: simpler HTTP tooling, caching, mobile and browser friendly, smaller payloads
Losses: formal contract discovery, some reliability and security standards
Criteria for decision: public API versus internal, transaction needs, existing client base
Migration path: wrap old services behind a gateway, move read paths first

bank.q: "Elasticity automatically saves money." Analyse this claim using scaling limits, cooldowns, warm-up time and billing granularity.
outline: Elasticity matches capacity to demand, but only between min and max
Cooldown and warm-up cause over-provisioning during fast surges
Billing is often per hour or per second; idle minimum instances still cost
Scaling the wrong metric (CPU for an IO-bound service) misfires
Evaluation: elasticity saves only with correct metrics, right limits and workload that actually varies

bank.q: A service claims 99.99% availability but depends on one region, one database and one ISP. Evaluate the claim and propose the architecture changes needed to support it.
outline: 99.99% allows about 4.3 minutes of downtime in 30 days
Single region and single database are single points of failure
Dependency chain: ISP path, provider edge, load balancer, DB
Proposals: replicas across zones, standby in a second region, DNS failover, health checks
Cost and consistency trade-offs; realistic target versus marketing claim

bank.q: Discuss the threats that appear when many tenants share one virtual server pool, and how hypervisors, network isolation and usage monitors reduce them.
outline: Tenant isolation at hypervisor level; escape and side-channel risks
Network separation: virtual networks, security groups, per-tenant VLANs
Storage isolation: separate volumes and encryption keys per tenant
Usage monitors detect abnormal consumption and abuse
Residual risk: shared CPU cache, misconfiguration exposing buckets or schemas

glossary.def: A geographic area in which a cloud provider runs one or more data centres, chosen for proximity to users or for legal reasons.
An isolated data-centre group inside a region, with its own power and network, so a failure in one zone does not take down another.
The time a request takes to travel to a server and back, measured in milliseconds.
An Internet Service Provider, the company that connects a customer's network to the rest of the Internet.
An Internet Exchange Point, a shared site where networks exchange traffic directly instead of through a backbone provider.
Running one copy of software for many customers, keeping each customer's data logically separate.
One customer or organisation in a multitenant system, identified by a tenant ID attached to its records and requests.
The Domain Name System, which resolves a name to an IP address using cached records with a time to live.
The request-response protocol of the web, in which a method and URL produce a status code and a body.
A stateless, resource-oriented style of using HTTP that most cloud APIs follow.
A property where each request carries all the information needed to process it, so the server keeps no session between calls.
Service-Oriented Architecture, a style in which loosely coupled services communicate through published contracts.
The published interface of a service: operations, message formats, endpoint and rules.
Automatic adjustment of capacity to match measured demand within set limits.
Adding or removing whole instances rather than making one machine bigger.
A rule that maps a metric, threshold, window and action into automatic capacity change, bounded by minimum and maximum.
A component that distributes incoming requests across a set of backend servers.
A periodic probe that decides whether a backend should keep receiving traffic.
Keeping identical copies of a service or data set so a lost copy can be replaced.
Moving traffic or the active role to a healthy copy after a failure.
A contract stating the promised service level, how it is measured, and the remedy if it is missed.
An internal target, stricter than the SLA, used by the team to run the service.
The fraction of time a service is usable, commonly quoted in nines such as 99.9%.
A software-defined computer with virtual CPU, memory and disk, running on a hypervisor.
The layer that creates, schedules and isolates virtual machines on a physical host.
Recording resource consumption per tenant in measured units so that billing can be calculated.
